marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q001.takeaway: Capillaries have an endothelial wall on a basal lamina and no adventitia.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q001.displayText:
The structure shown is a capillary. Its wall is formed mainly by endothelial cells lined externally by a glycoprotein basal lamina. It has no adventitia, distinguishing it from a venule.

Capillaries are classified as:
• Continuous — endothelial edges of adjoining cells fuse to form a continuous wall. Material exchanges through endothelial-cell cytoplasm or intercellular material.
• Fenestrated — apertures in the endothelium are closed by a thin diaphragm; pores may extend through the full endothelial thickness. Material exchanges by diffusion through fenestrations. They are found mainly in renal glomeruli, intestinal villi, endocrine glands and pancreas.

Sinusoids differ from capillaries because their wall has endothelium supported by a thin layer of connective tissue. Their endothelium has larger deficiencies in the form of fenestrations or long slits.

rationales.a: Arteries have a prominent multi-layered wall and smooth-muscle/elastic media; the shown endothelial tube without adventitia is a capillary.
rationales.b: Venules are larger post-capillary vessels with connective-tissue support/adventitia; the capillary has endothelium and basal lamina without adventitia.
rationales.d: Arterioles have a smooth-muscle layer and are not the thin endothelial-only exchange vessels shown.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q002.takeaway: Arterial adventitial collagen runs longitudinally; media muscle or elastic elements run circularly.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q002.displayText:
In arteries, the fibrous elements of the tunica intima and adventitia (mainly collagen) run longitudinally, along the vessel. In the tunica media, elastic tissue or muscle runs circularly. The adventitia contains prominent collagen and prevents undue stretching or distension.

From inside outward, the arterial wall has three layers:
1. Tunica intima — endothelium on a basal lamina, with delicate subendothelial connective tissue. A membrane of elastic fibers, the internal elastic lamina, surrounds this layer.
2. Tunica media — smooth muscle or elastic tissue, determining whether the artery is muscular or elastic. These tissues are surrounded by the external elastic lamina.
3. Tunica adventitia — the outermost layer, predominantly connective tissue with collagen fibers; it prevents overstretching and excessive distension.

rationales.a: The intima’s collagenous subendothelial tissue and adventitial collagen run longitudinally; the media’s muscle/elastic tissue runs circularly.
rationales.c: Collagen is prominent in adventitia, whereas media is primarily smooth muscle or elastic tissue depending on the artery.
rationales.d: The intima includes endothelium and delicate subendothelial connective tissue; prominent collagen is in adventitia.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q003.takeaway: Elastic arteries recoil during diastole to sustain blood flow between heartbeats.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q003.displayText:
Elastic-artery recoil helps maintain continuous blood flow. Large elastic arteries distend and recoil during systole and diastole because they contain abundant elastic tissue. Recoil provides an additional force that pushes blood into smaller arteries, so flow continues with some pressure fluctuation between systole and diastole.

The source table compares elastic and muscular arteries: the internal elastic lamina is not distinguishable from the surrounding media in elastic arteries but is distinct in muscular arteries; elastic arteries have predominantly elastic fibers and few smooth-muscle cells in the media, while muscular arteries have predominantly smooth muscle and very few elastic fibers. Elastic arteries have a relatively thin adventitia consisting mainly of elastic fibers; muscular arteries have a relatively thick adventitia consisting of fibroblastic tissue.

Elastic arteries are conducting vessels; muscular arteries are distributing vessels. The elastic-artery tunica media is predominantly elastic tissue, with some loose connective tissue and possibly some smooth-muscle cells.

rationales.a: Elastic arteries are conducting vessels; muscular arteries are the distributing arteries.
rationales.b: The internal elastic lamina blends with the media in elastic arteries; it is distinct in muscular arteries.
rationales.c: Elastic arteries do contain some smooth-muscle cells, although elastic tissue predominates in their media.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q004.takeaway: The lymph-node mapping is capsule, subcapsular sinus, germinal centre, lymphoid nodule and trabeculae.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q004.displayText:
The marked lymph-node structures are:
1 — capsule
2 — subcapsular sinus
3 — germinal centre
4 — lymphoid nodule
5 — trabeculae

Each lymph node has a connective-tissue framework and many lymphocytes arranged in a reticulin-fiber and cell stroma. Its three major regions are:
• Cortex — subcapsular sinuses, lymphoid nodules and densely packed lymphocytes; it stains darkly. Each nodule has a lightly stained germinal centre surrounded by densely packed lymphocytes.
• Paracortex — lacks nodules and has fewer lymphocytes, so it stains lightly.
• Medulla — has prominent draining sinusoids adjacent to the hilum.

rationales.a: The mapping is not correct: label 2 is the subcapsular sinus, 3 is the germinal centre, and 4 the lymphoid nodule.
rationales.b: This mapping assigns 1 and 2 incorrectly; the capsule is 1 and the subcapsular sinus is 2.
rationales.d: The capsule is 1, not 2; the remaining listed structures also do not match these labels.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q005.takeaway: Splenic arterioles branch into straight vessels called penicilli.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q005.displayText:
Splenic arterioles divide into straight vessels called penicilli. The splenic artery divides at the hilum into about five branches, which enter independently and subdivide through the trabecular network. Arterioles leave the trabeculae and pass into intertrabecular spaces.

The spleen is composed of:
• White pulp — for some distance each arteriole is surrounded by a dense lymphocyte sheath.
• Penicilli — straight vessels into which the arteriole divides.
• Ellipsoid — a localized thickening in each penicillus wall, with concentric lamellae formed by aggregated fibroblasts and macrophages.
• Ampulla — distal to the ellipsoid, the vessel dilates and its wall becomes continuous with the reticular framework.
• Red pulp — blood flows into spaces lined by reticular cells, directly contacting lymphocytes; this blood-infiltrated tissue is red pulp.
• Sinusoids — wide sinusoids collect red-pulp blood and drain to veins in the trabeculae.

Splenic sinusoids are lined by modified endothelium; their elongated endothelial cells are called stave cells.

rationales.a: Stave cells line splenic sinusoids; the straight vessels formed by arterioles are penicilli.
rationales.b: An ellipsoid is the localized wall thickening on a penicillus, not the straight vessel itself.
rationales.d: An ampulla is the dilated segment distal to an ellipsoid, rather than the straight arteriolar vessel.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q006.takeaway: A corpuscle of Hassall in the thymic medulla identifies thymic tissue.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q006.displayText: The sample is thymus, identified by a corpuscle of Hassall. These small, rounded structures are formed from eosinophilic type VI epithelial reticular cells in the thymic medulla. Each corpuscle has a central core of degenerated epithelial cells that appears as a pink-stained hyaline mass, surrounded by concentrically arranged epithelial cells that stain bright pink with H&E.

rationales.a: The spleen has white and red pulp but not thymic Hassall corpuscles.
rationales.b: Palatine tonsil is MALT; Hassall corpuscles are found in thymic medulla.
rationales.d: Bone marrow is not characterized by Hassall corpuscles; those structures identify thymus.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q007.takeaway: Ileal Peyer’s patches are aggregated MALT follicles in the submucosa.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q007.displayText:
The marked structure in the ileal section is mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), also called gut-associated lymphoid tissue. In the ileum, it appears as aggregated lymphatic follicles (Peyer’s patches) in the submucosa.

Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue is also found in other regions:
• Tonsils are collections of lymphoid tissue near the junction of the oral cavity and pharynx. The largest are the right and left palatine tonsils, on either side of the oropharyngeal isthmus.
• Solitary lymphatic follicles are small collections similar in structure to lymph-node follicles and may occur anywhere along the gut.
• Aggregated lymphatic follicles (Peyer’s patches) are larger groups of 10–200 follicles in the small intestine. The source image shows Peyer’s patches in ileal submucosa.

rationales.a: Thymus is identified by Hassall corpuscles; the marked ileal aggregates are MALT.
rationales.b: Splenic white/red pulp is not the ileal submucosal Peyer’s-patch tissue shown.
rationales.d: A lymph node has nodules and sinuses, whereas the ileal aggregate is gut-associated MALT.

reconstruction.reconstructedContent:
The marked structure in the ileal section is mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), also called gut-associated lymphoid tissue. In the ileum, it appears as aggregated lymphatic follicles (Peyer’s patches) in the submucosa.

Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue is also found in other regions:
• Tonsils are collections of lymphoid tissue near the junction of the oral cavity and pharynx. The largest are the right and left palatine tonsils, on either side of the oropharyngeal isthmus.
• Solitary lymphatic follicles are small collections similar in structure to lymph-node follicles and may occur anywhere along the gut.
• Aggregated lymphatic follicles (Peyer’s patches) are larger groups of 10–200 follicles in the small intestine. The source image shows Peyer’s patches in ileal submucosa.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q008.takeaway: Olfactory sustentacular cells are supporting cells with apical microvilli and lipofuscin pigment.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q008.displayText: Sustentacular cells are the supporting cells of the olfactory epithelium. Their oval nuclei lie near the epithelial free surface, which bears numerous microvilli embedded in overlying mucus. The cytoplasm contains yellow lipofuscin pigment that gives the olfactory mucosa its yellow color. In addition to supporting the olfactory epithelium, sustentacular cells are phagocytic; their pigment may represent remnants of phagocytosed olfactory cells.

rationales.a: Olfactory receptor cells are the sensory neurons, not the supporting sustentacular cells.
rationales.c: Olfactory receptor cells detect odorants; sustentacular cells provide epithelial support.
rationales.d: Basal cells are stem/progenitor cells near the epithelial base, whereas sustentacular cells are apical supporting cells.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q009.takeaway: Trachea is identified by respiratory epithelium, seromucous glands and hyaline cartilage.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q009.displayText:
The histological image shows trachea, identified by pseudostratified ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium, seromucous glands and hyaline cartilage. A tracheal section includes respiratory epithelium, basement membrane, submucosal serous and mucous glands, perichondrium, tracheal cartilage and trachealis smooth muscle.

Bronchi differ from the trachea by having cartilage plates rather than rings and a smooth-muscle layer between the lamina propria and submucosa. In smaller branches, cartilage decreases while smooth muscle increases; the number of glands and goblet cells also decreases. The source also shows a bronchus section for comparison.

rationales.b: Bronchi have cartilage plates and a smooth-muscle layer between lamina propria and submucosa, unlike the tracheal ring pattern.
rationales.c: Bronchioles lack cartilage and submucosal glands; the section has tracheal cartilage and seromucous glands.
rationales.d: Alveoli are thin-walled gas-exchange spaces and do not show tracheal cartilage, glands and respiratory epithelium together.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q010.takeaway: Alveolar ducts connect respiratory bronchioles to alveolar sacs.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q010.displayText:
The marked structure is the lumen of an alveolar duct. These tiny ducts connect respiratory bronchioles to alveolar sacs, each containing a collection of alveoli (small mucus-lined pouches made of flattened epithelial cells).

The conducting-to-respiratory passage sequence is: principal bronchus → secondary (lobar) bronchi → tertiary (segmental) bronchi → lobular bronchioles → terminal bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles are the most distal conducting passages; each divides into respiratory bronchioles, each of which divides into a few alveolar ducts. Each alveolar duct ends in an atrium leading to rounded alveolar sacs, which are studded with alveoli. The colored strips in the source image show the distribution of different cells and structures along the tracheobronchial tree.

rationales.a: An alveolus is a small air space in an alveolar sac, not the ductal passage connecting respiratory bronchioles to the sacs.
rationales.c: Respiratory bronchioles precede alveolar ducts in the airway sequence; the marked lumen is the duct.
rationales.d: Terminal bronchioles are conducting passages and are proximal to respiratory bronchioles, not alveolar ducts.

marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q011.takeaway: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and bear apical microvilli.
marrow__ANAT_CH14_Q011.displayText:
The rounded secretory cells bearing microvilli on the alveolar lining are type II pneumocytes.

The main alveolar lining cells are:
• Type I pneumocytes — large, flattened cells forming a very thin gas-diffusion barrier; they are connected by tight junctions.
• Type II pneumocytes — rounded secretory cells with microvilli on their free surfaces. They secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse during respiration.
• Type III alveolar cells (brush cells) — their function is not clearly known.

rationales.a: Type I pneumocytes are flattened gas-diffusion cells, not the rounded secretory cells with microvilli.
rationales.c: “Alveolar cells” is a general term; the specifically described surfactant-secreting rounded cells are type II pneumocytes.
rationales.d: Brush cells are type III alveolar cells; their function is unclear, while type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant.
